source: E. B. Cowell and J. Eggeling, Catalogue of Buddhist Sanskrit Manuscripts in the possession of the Royal Asiatic Society (Hodgson Collection), JRAS 8.1 (1875), pp. 1-52; parsed from uploaded OCR/VL scan
source_control: The catalogue states at the outset that the manuscript material is Indian paper unless otherwise stated. Therefore 'default paper' is a declared catalogue baseline and is not expected to be repeated in every individual entry.

support_exceptions.blackened_paper_note: MS 77 is described as 21 leaves of blackened paper, written in alternating yellow and white paint/lines; MSS 78-79 inherit size/paper/hand from the preceding manuscript by cross-reference.

high_information_form_exceptions.feature: 46 leaves in one continuous roll; writing covers 69 pages
wrapper mentioned as a title/identity surface
collection title explicitly reported from wrapper
69 palm leaves; title stated to be given on wrapper only
40 leaves folded into one continuous roll; work called by title on wrapper
ticket pasted on back of last leaf carries descriptive/donor note

photographic_plate_features: old dated manuscripts reproduced photographically for scholarly comparison
text columns separated by blank stripes containing cord holes
facsimile date numerals added to blank stripe in reproduction
reproduction therefore selects and augments visible material features rather than functioning as a transparent copy
interpretation: Material description is systematic rather than occasional: leaf count, dimensions and line density are recorded for almost the entire 79-entry corpus.
Support follows a baseline/exception information economy: Indian paper is the declared default; palm leaf and treated/special paper states are explicitly marked.
Rare wrapper, pasted-ticket and folding notes carry unusually high evidential value because they record identity/provenance/form relations not contained in the text alone.
The catalogue converts unique manuscript paper objects into portable descriptive tuples for remote scholarly identification and comparison.
The near-universal recording of form metrics makes this a strong case of material codicology functioning as nineteenth-century scholarly infrastructure.
method_warning: Counts are derived from OCR-parsed headings and descriptors. Exact entry wording and numerical typography should be verified against page images before publication quotation. The overall coverage counts are robust enough for corpus-level orientation because the catalogue structure is highly regular.
